# Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion

The term "Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion" refers not to a single, unique structure but to at least two distinct and geographically separate chapels in the United States that share this name , . Both chapels are named for the biblical figure, St. Cornelius the Centurion, whose conversion marked a pivotal moment in Christian history by establishing the precedent for the inclusion of Gentiles into the Church on equal terms with Jewish converts , . The first chapel is an English Gothic-style masonry building located on Governors Island in New York Harbor, constructed in 1906 to replace an earlier wooden chapel from 1847 , . It stands within a National Historic Landmark District and has undergone significant adaptive reuse, now serving as a venue for contemporary art installations while remaining publicly accessible , . The second chapel is a wood-frame Gothic Revival structure located within Fort Monroe in Hampton, Virginia; it was consecrated in 1858 and holds the distinction of being the U.S. Army's oldest wooden building used continuously for religious services , . Its construction was funded through private subscription following a personal act of gratitude by a surviving officer after a laboratory explosion , . While both chapels honor the same saint, their histories, architectural styles, funding origins, and current statuses are markedly different, reflecting unique developments within their respective military and civilian contexts.

## Governors Island Chapel, New York City

The Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion on Governors Island represents a complex history of military service, ecclesiastical transition, and civic transformation, culminating in its current role as a preserved historic landmark and cultural venue. Its narrative begins with a modest wooden predecessor, which itself arose from the growing need for a permanent Episcopal presence on the island's U.S. military installation , . The initial chapel was erected in 1847 under the dedicated leadership of Reverend John McVickar, who had been commissioned as the post chaplain at Fort Columbus in 1844 , . The project was a collaborative effort, receiving continuous support from Trinity Church in Manhattan, a major financial backer alongside McVickar's own personal contributions , . The dedication of this first chapel occurred on April 19, 1847, officiated by Bishop William H. DeLancey of the Episcopal Diocese of Western New York . The cost of this initial construction is reported with some variation across sources, with figures cited as $2,500 (a 1950 source), $4,500 (a 1973 source), or a more substantial $25,000 as mentioned in a letter from McVickar himself in 1846 . Over time, this wooden structure fell into disrepair and was ultimately condemned by the early 20th century, necessitating the construction of a more durable replacement .

This replacement was the current chapel, a significant architectural undertaking designed by the American architect Charles Coolidge Haight , . Construction took place between 1905 and 1906, marking a new era for the chapel and the island , . The cornerstone for the new building was laid on October 27, 1905, by Coadjutor Bishop David H. Greer of the Episcopal Diocese of New York, and the chapel was formally consecrated on October 19, 1906 , . The choice of Haight, a Union Army veteran who served under General Winfield Scott Hancock, may have been influenced by his military background, leading him to incorporate integrated military motifs, such as turrets, into the design of the chapel, which stood as a prominent feature on the former army base . The chapel was built on the site of the original 1847 structure, and photographs from the period show the old and new buildings standing contemporaneously, with the new stone edifice positioned behind its wooden predecessor . The chapel is situated in the Noland Park section of Governors Island, a location administered by the Governors Island Preservation and Education Corporation since January 31, 2003, following the island's transfer from the U.S. federal government , . This entire area, including the chapel, is designated as both a National Historic Landmark District and a New York City Historic District, underscoring its significant historical and architectural value .

Architecturally, the chapel is a prime example of the English Gothic style of the 14th century, specifically executed in the Gothic Revival tradition , . Constructed from buff Indiana limestone, the building measures approximately 106 feet in length and 70 feet in its greatest width , . Its cruciform plan consists of a nave, transepts, and a chancel , . A defining external feature is its three-story northwest tower, which is crowned with a four-turret parapet and surmounted by a slate roof with copper gutters . The exterior is punctuated by 35 lancet-shaped stained glass windows, adding to its visual grandeur . The interior retains white walls and houses a pipe organ . Beneath the chancel lies a vaulted crypt and mortuary chapel, which features flat Italian tile roofing . The chapel also includes carved oak clergy and choir seats, contributing to its traditional liturgical setting . Architectural Preservation Studio was retained by Trinity Real Estate to conduct a comprehensive conditions assessment of the chapel, which included laser-scanning documentation of both the exterior and interior to produce highly accurate drawings for preservation purposes .

The chapel's ownership and operational history reflects the broader shifts in governance of Governors Island. Initially, the War Department provided chaplains and supported the facility . However, a pivotal change occurred in 1868 when the War Department ceased providing chaplains, at which point the chapel became a free chapel operating directly under the control of Trinity Parish . This transition solidified its identity as part of the parish rather than solely a military installation. In 1954, the chapel's use was expanded to include interdenominational Protestant services, broadening its community reach beyond its original Episcopal focus . The chapel's relationship with the U.S. government reached a critical juncture in 1986, when Trinity Church formally donated the chapel to the U.S. Government . Crucially, this donation was made with a reversion clause, stipulating that ownership would revert to Trinity if the land was ever returned to civilian use or if the chapel ceased to be used for a military purpose . When the U.S. Coast Guard vacated Governors Island in 1996, this trigger was activated, and ownership legally reverted to Trinity Church, which has retained ownership to this day , . Since that time, the chapel has been inactive for regular worship services . Prior to its closure for worship, its nave displayed historic regimental flags, which were later relocated to the U.S. Army Center of Military History in Washington, D.C., in the 1980s . The chapel's dedication to St. Cornelius the Centurion is reinforced through its liturgical elements, including a reredos with three military saints featuring Cornelius prominently on the right and a stained glass window depicting the biblical scene from Acts 10 . The chapel's continued existence as a publicly accessible space and its integration into the island's cultural programming represent a successful adaptive reuse, transforming a former military chapel into a vibrant public destination .

## Chapel of the Centurion, Fort Monroe, Virginia

The Chapel of the Centurion at Fort Monroe in Hampton, Virginia, presents a narrative of enduring continuity, distinguished by its age, unique founding story, and unbroken service as a place of worship for the U.S. military. Unlike its counterpart in New York, this chapel was never replaced; it began life as a permanent wooden structure and has served continuously for religious services since its consecration in 1858 , . Its construction was initiated in 1855 following a tragic event at the fort's arsenal—a laboratory explosion that killed two men but spared Lieutenant Julian McAllister , . McAllister attributed his survival to divine intervention and, as a result, he commissioned the chapel and served as its principal donor, raising $6,000 through private subscription to fund its construction , . This compelling origin story, rooted in personal faith and military experience, imbues the chapel with a unique historical character . The chapel was designed by the renowned Gothic Revival architect Richard Upjohn, one of America's most influential architects of the 19th century , . His plans, published in his 1852 pattern book 'Rural Architecture', were modified for the site, extending the structure to five bays to accommodate a congregation of 200-225 people . The chapel was completed in 1857 and officially consecrated on May 3, 1858, by Bishop John Johns of St. John's Episcopal Church in Hampton , .

Architecturally, the chapel is a notable example of Upjohn's work, executed in the wood-frame Gothic Revival style , . As one of the oldest wooden churches built on a U.S. Army post, it holds a special place in American architectural history , . The chapel is located within the walls of Old Fort Monroe, at Old Point Comfort, on the edge of the Parade Ground facing northeast . It stands adjacent to the Casemate Museum and other historic structures within the fort complex, which is now a National Monument administered by the National Park Service and the Fort Monroe Authority , . The chapel's interior features three stained-glass memorial windows, which are attributed to the famous artist Louis Comfort Tiffany and his Tiffany Glass and Decorating Company of New York City, adding a significant artistic dimension to its simple wooden frame . The chapel is named for Cornelius the Centurion, the Roman military officer who, according to the biblical account in Acts 10, was the first documented Gentile convert to Christianity, a theological principle of universal inclusion that resonates deeply within the context of a military garrison , . Above the altar is a stained-glass window that depicts the biblical scene of Cornelius sending for Peter, visually connecting the chapel's mission to its foundational story .

The chapel's long history is intertwined with the military and religious life of Fort Monroe. Regular religious services at the fort began as early as 1825 under Reverend Mark Chevers, rector of St. John's Episcopal Church, who served as the official post chaplain from December 1, 1838, until his death in 1875 , . Following the chapel's consecration, it became the primary venue for Protestant, non-denominational worship services conducted by U.S. Army post chaplains . The chapel has seen several periods of restoration and maintenance over the years, including repairs after fire damage and pipe organ replacement in 1933, and an extensive restoration project guided by historical research from April 1968 to April 1969, which cost $200,000 to ensure authenticity to the original 1858 structure . It also underwent exterior repainting to a white finish with green trim in 1946 . The chapel's ecclesiastical jurisdiction is unique; while the physical building remains property of the United States government, its sacramental records—including baptisms, confirmations, marriages, and funerals—are maintained centrally by the Archdiocese for the Military Services (AMS) . The AMS serves as the canonical authority for Catholic chaplains in the U.S. Armed Forces and oversees all Catholic liturgy and religious education programs within military chapels . This administrative framework ensures the proper recording of sacraments performed within the chapel's walls, even though it operates on military land. As of September 2024, the chapel remains in active use for civilian religious services, continuing its long tradition of spiritual ministry .

## Theological Foundation: St. Cornelius the Centurion

The naming of both the Governors Island and Fort Monroe chapels after St. Cornelius the Centurion is not arbitrary but is rooted in a profound theological significance derived from his biblical story, which is recounted in the Book of Acts , . St. Cornelius was a Roman centurion, a military officer commanding a cohort, stationed in Caesarea, the capital of the Roman province of Judea during the 1st century CE , , . He is described in Acts 10 as a devout man who "feared God," gave alms generously to the Jewish people, and prayed constantly , , . His piety placed him in a category known as a "proselyte of the gate"—a Gentile sympathetic to Judaism who worshipped the God of Israel but had not converted fully through circumcision or adherence to the Mosaic ceremonial law , . This characterization is crucial, as it establishes him as a seeker of the true God outside the established covenant community of Israel, yet open to divine revelation . His devotion was so consistent that it is noted he prayed at the ninth hour, around 3:00 PM, aligning his practice with the established times for prayer in the Jewish temple , , .

The pivotal event in Cornelius's life, and in the history of the early Christian Church, occurs when he receives a vision from an angel of God , . The angel instructs him to send men to Joppa to find Simon Peter and bring him back to Cornelius's house , . At the very same time, Peter, who is in Joppa, receives a parallel vision while preparing for lunch . He sees a great sheet descending from heaven containing all kinds of animals, both clean and unclean according to Jewish dietary laws, and hears a voice command him to "kill and eat" , . Peter objects, stating that he has never eaten anything considered "common or unclean" . The voice responds, "What God has made clean, you must not call profane" , , . This vision is repeated three times, signifying its divine import . Later, the Holy Spirit tells Peter that three men are seeking him and instructs him to go with them without hesitation, as the visit is divinely sanctioned .

When Peter arrives at Cornelius's home, he preaches to Cornelius and his assembled household, which includes relatives and close friends , . As Peter speaks, the Holy Spirit falls upon all who are listening, just as it did at Pentecost , . They begin to speak in tongues and praise God . Witnessing this miraculous outpouring of the Spirit, Peter recognizes it as proof of God's acceptance of the Gentiles and commands that they be baptized "in the name of Jesus Christ" , . This baptism marks the first recorded conversion and baptism of uncircumcised Gentiles into the Christian Church, a watershed moment that inaugurated the mission to the Gentiles , , . The event triggered significant debate among the Jewish Christians in Jerusalem, who questioned whether Gentiles could be admitted to the Church without requiring circumcision , . Peter's defense of his actions, highlighting the direct descent of the Holy Spirit, eventually led to a formal resolution at the Council of Jerusalem, which decreed that Gentile converts were not required to follow Jewish ceremonial laws , .

Post-biblical traditions elaborate further on Cornelius's life. Eastern Orthodox hagiography, in texts like the 'Martyrium of Cornelius the Centurion', states that after his conversion, he retired from the army, accompanied St. Peter on missionary journeys, and was later sent alone to Skepsis in Mysia where he confronted local paganism , . According to this tradition, he miraculously restored a prince’s wife and child from rubble after an earthquake destroyed the temple of Zeus, leading to mass conversions and his appointment as bishop of Skepsis by Peter , . He is said to have died there as a martyr in old age, buried near the ruins of the pagan temple , . These traditions, while not part of the canonical scripture, reinforce his status as a foundational figure in the expansion of Christianity beyond its Jewish origins. His feast day is observed on February 4 in the Episcopal Church calendar, and he is venerated as the patron saint of soldiers, benefactors, philanthropists, and Jewish converts , . The theological principles embodied by his story—divine initiative in calling seekers, the abolition of ritual distinctions between Jew and Gentile, and the universality of salvation—are precisely why military chapels, symbols of service and duty, would choose to honor him. His life exemplifies radical hospitality, openness to divine guidance, and the breaking down of social and religious barriers, making him a powerful and fitting patron for institutions dedicated to the spiritual well-being of diverse communities , .

## Comparative Analysis of the Chapels

While both the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion on Governors Island and the Chapel of the Centurion at Fort Monroe share a common name and theological inspiration, they are distinct entities with divergent histories, architectural identities, and roles in their respective communities. A comparative analysis reveals how two similar names can mask fundamentally different stories of development, purpose, and adaptation. The most immediate difference lies in their construction and material. The Governors Island chapel, in its current form, is a large, permanent masonry structure built of buff Indiana limestone between 1905 and 1906 , . It was a replacement for a deteriorating 1847 wooden chapel, representing a significant investment in a more durable and imposing building , . In stark contrast, the Chapel of the Centurion at Fort Monroe is a wood-frame Gothic Revival building, completed in 1858 and consecrated in 1858 , . It was the original chapel from its inception and has remained in continuous use without replacement, making it a rare and invaluable artifact of 19th-century American ecclesiastical architecture on a military post , .

Their founding narratives and funding mechanisms also differ significantly. The Governors Island chapel originated from the organized efforts of the Episcopal Church and Trinity Parish, with initial funding coming from donors and the personal contributions of chaplain John McVickar , . Its establishment was a response to the needs of a growing military population. The Fort Monroe chapel, however, has a more dramatic and personal origin story. Its construction was directly funded by private subscription led by Lieutenant Julian McAllister, who survived a fatal laboratory explosion at the fort and attributed his safety to divine intervention , , . His role as the principal contributor provides a compelling human element to the chapel's history, linking its foundation to a moment of profound personal faith and gratitude . This narrative of a single officer's vow gives the chapel a unique and intimate backstory compared to the more institutionalized founding of its New York counterpart.

Architecturally, the chapels reflect different tastes and eras. The Governors Island chapel, designed by Charles C. Haight, showcases a robust English Gothic style of the late 19th century, characterized by its massive limestone construction, a prominent three-story tower, and numerous stained glass windows , . Haight's design incorporated subtle military motifs, likely reflecting his own background and the chapel's setting on a former army base . The Fort Monroe chapel, designed by the celebrated architect Richard Upjohn, embodies the refined elegance of the mid-19th-century Gothic Revival movement . Its simpler wood-frame construction belies its artistic importance, particularly due to the presence of three stained-glass windows attributed to Louis Comfort Tiffany, a master of the medium . This highlights the different aesthetic priorities and available resources at the time of their construction. The Governors Island chapel is a monumental statement of permanence, while the Fort Monroe chapel is a testament to the enduring beauty of a carefully crafted wooden structure.

Perhaps the most significant difference lies in their modern histories and current statuses. The chapel on Governors Island has undergone a complete transformation from a military chapel to a public cultural venue. After being inactive for worship since the Coast Guard's departure in 1996, it has been repurposed as a site for contemporary art installations, such as Jacob Hashimoto’s 'The Eclipse' , . This adaptive reuse aligns with the broader redevelopment of Governors Island into a public park and cultural destination, managed by the Governors Island Preservation and Education Corporation , . In contrast, the chapel at Fort Monroe continues its original function as an active place of worship. As of September 2024, it remains in active use for civilian religious services, maintaining its role as a spiritual center for the community connected to the former military base, now a national monument . This ongoing use preserves its original intent far more directly than its New York counterpart. Their paths of ownership also diverge; the Governors Island chapel was transferred to the city and then reclaimed by its original church owner, Trinity Church, which now manages it as a historic asset , . The Fort Monroe chapel, meanwhile, remains on government property, with its sacramental records handled by the Archdiocese for the Military Services, illustrating a different model of stewardship for a chapel on active-duty land .

## Current Status and Preservation

The current state of the two chapels named for St. Cornelius the Centurion reflects their divergent paths from active military chapels to their present-day incarnations. The chapel on Governors Island in New York City has successfully navigated a transition from a functional place of worship to a preserved historic landmark and a dynamic public cultural venue. Following the U.S. Coast Guard's departure from the island in 1996, the chapel became inactive for regular religious services . However, its historical significance ensured its preservation. As part of the Governors Island National Historic Landmark District and New York City Historic District, the chapel is protected and maintained as a key component of the island's heritage . Ownership reverted to Trinity Church, which has since managed the property , . Recognizing the potential of the space, the chapel has been repurposed for contemporary use. It is now publicly accessible and serves as a venue for art installations and cultural programming, a role that aligns with the island's transformation into a major public park and arts destination . Notably, the chapel hosted Jacob Hashimoto’s 'The Eclipse', a suspended monochrome disk installation adapted from the 57th Venice Biennale, as part of the Governors Island Art Fair programming . This adaptive reuse demonstrates a creative approach to preservation, ensuring the building remains a vibrant and relevant part of the community while honoring its past. The chapel's architectural integrity has been assessed by professionals like the Architectural Preservation Studio, which conducted a comprehensive conditions evaluation, including laser-scanning documentation to create precise drawings for future conservation efforts . This commitment to preservation ensures that the chapel will continue to stand as a significant example of 19th-century ecclesiastical architecture for future generations.

In contrast, the Chapel of the Centurion at Fort Monroe has maintained its core function as a place of active worship, adapting to the changing landscape of Fort Monroe itself. Fort Monroe, once a sprawling U.S. Army base, was decommissioned and transformed into a combined National Monument and Presidential Site managed by the National Park Service and the Fort Monroe Authority , . Despite this significant change in administration and purpose for the surrounding area, the chapel has continued its uninterrupted service as a place of worship. As of September 2024, it remains in active use for civilian religious services, fulfilling its original mission . This continuity is remarkable, especially considering the chapel's age and its location within a complex undergoing major redevelopment. The chapel's status is further secured by its unique administrative arrangement with the Archdiocese for the Military Services (AMS). While the physical building is owned by the U.S. government, the AMS maintains canonical oversight and centralizes all sacramental records performed within it, ensuring that the chapel's religious functions are properly documented and sustained . This partnership between a civilian governing body and a specialized ecclesiastical authority allows the chapel to operate effectively on military land. The chapel's physical condition has been maintained through periodic restoration projects, including a major effort in 1968-1969 that cost $200,000 and was meticulously researched to preserve its historical authenticity . This ongoing commitment to preservation and active use underscores the chapel's enduring importance to the community and its successful integration into the new civilian identity of Fort Monroe. To summarize, while both chapels are historic treasures, the Governors Island chapel has embraced a new role as a cultural institution, whereas the Fort Monroe chapel has persevered as a living, breathing center of faith and community.

It stands adjacent to the Casemate Museum and other historic structures within the fort complex, which is now a National Monument administered by the National Park Service and the Fort Monroe Authority.

The chapel's interior features three stained-glass memorial windows, which are attributed to the famous artist Louis Comfort Tiffany and his Tiffany Glass and Decorating Company of New York City, adding a significant artistic dimension to its simple wooden frame.

The chapel is named for Cornelius the Centurion, the Roman military officer who, according to the biblical account in Acts 10, was the first documented Gentile convert to Christianity, a theological principle of universal inclusion that resonates deeply within the context of a military garrison.
Above the altar is a stained-glass window that depicts the biblical scene of Cornelius sending for Peter, visually connecting the chapel's mission to its foundational story.

Regular religious services at Fort Monroe began as early as 1825 under Reverend Mark Chevers, rector of St. John's Episcopal Church, who served as the official post chaplain from December 1, 1838, until his death in 1875.
Following the chapel's consecration, it became the primary venue for Protestant, non-denominational worship services conducted by U.S. Army post chaplains.

The chapel has seen several periods of restoration and maintenance over the years, including repairs after fire damage and pipe organ replacement in 1933, and an extensive restoration project guided by historical research from April 1968 to April 1969, which cost $200,000 to ensure authenticity to the original 1858 structure.
It also underwent exterior repainting to a white finish with green trim in 1946.

The chapel's ecclesiastical jurisdiction is unique; while the physical building remains property of the United States government, its sacramental records—including baptisms, confirmations, marriages, and funerals—are maintained centrally by the Archdiocese for the Military Services (AMS).
The AMS serves as the canonical authority for Catholic chaplains in the U.S. Armed Forces and oversees all Catholic liturgy and religious education programs within military chapels.
This administrative framework ensures the proper recording of sacraments performed within the chapel's walls, even though it operates on military land.
As of September 2024, the chapel remains in active use for civilian religious services, continuing its long tradition of spiritual ministry.

The naming of both the Governors Island and Fort Monroe chapels after St. Cornelius the Centurion is not arbitrary but is rooted in a profound theological significance derived from his biblical story, which is recounted in the Book of Acts.
St. Cornelius was a Roman centurion, a military officer commanding a cohort, stationed in Caesarea, the capital of the Roman province of Judea during the 1st century CE.
He is described in Acts 10 as a devout man who "feared God," gave alms generously to the Jewish people, and prayed constantly.

His piety placed him in a category known as a "proselyte of the gate"—a Gentile sympathetic to Judaism who worshipped the God of Israel but had not converted fully through circumcision or adherence to the Mosaic ceremonial law.
This characterization is crucial, as it establishes him as a seeker of the true God outside the established covenant community of Israel, yet open to divine revelation.
His devotion was so consistent that it is noted he prayed at the ninth hour, around 3:00 PM, aligning his practice with the established times for prayer in the Jewish temple.
The pivotal event in Cornelius's life, and in the history of the early Christian Church, occurs when he receives a vision from an angel of God.
The angel instructs him to send men to Joppa to find Simon Peter and bring him back to Cornelius's house.
At the very same time, Peter, who is in Joppa, receives a parallel vision while preparing for lunch.
He sees a great sheet descending from heaven containing all kinds of animals, both clean and unclean according to Jewish dietary laws, and hears a voice command him to "kill and eat".
Peter objects, stating that he has never eaten anything considered "common or unclean".
The voice responds, "What God has made clean, you must not call profane".
This vision is repeated three times, signifying its divine import.
Later, the Holy Spirit tells Peter that three men are seeking him and instructs him to go with them without hesitation, as the visit is divinely sanctioned.
When Peter arrives at Cornelius's home, he preaches to Cornelius and his assembled household, which includes relatives and close friends.
As Peter speaks, the Holy Spirit falls upon all who are listening, just as it did at Pentecost.
They begin to speak in tongues and praise God.
Witnessing this miraculous outpouring of the Spirit, Peter recognizes it as proof of God's acceptance of the Gentiles and commands that they be baptized "in the name of Jesus Christ".
This baptism marks the first recorded conversion and baptism of uncircumcised Gentiles into the Christian Church, a watershed moment that inaugurated the mission to the Gentiles.
The event triggered significant debate among the Jewish Christians in Jerusalem, who questioned whether Gentiles could be admitted to the Church without requiring circumcision.

Peter's defense of his actions, highlighting the direct descent of the Holy Spirit, eventually led to a formal resolution at the Council of Jerusalem, which decreed that Gentile converts were not required to follow Jewish ceremonial laws.

Eastern Orthodox hagiography, in texts like the 'Martyrium of Cornelius the Centurion', states that after his conversion, he retired from the army, accompanied St. Peter on missionary journeys, and was later sent alone to Skepsis in Mysia where he confronted local paganism.

According to this tradition, he miraculously restored a prince’s wife and child from rubble after an earthquake destroyed the temple of Zeus, leading to mass conversions and his appointment as bishop of Skepsis by Peter.
He is said to have died there as a martyr in old age, buried near the ruins of the pagan temple.
These traditions, while not part of the canonical scripture, reinforce his status as a foundational figure in the expansion of Christianity beyond its Jewish origins.
His feast day is observed on February 4 in the Episcopal Church calendar, and he is venerated as the patron saint of soldiers, benefactors, philanthropists, and Jewish converts.

The theological principles embodied by his story—divine initiative in calling seekers, the abolition of ritual distinctions between Jew and Gentile, and the universality of salvation—are precisely why military chapels, symbols of service and duty, would choose to honor him.

His life exemplifies radical hospitality, openness to divine guidance, and the breaking down of social and religious barriers, making him a powerful and fitting patron for institutions dedicated to the spiritual well-being of diverse communities.
The Governors Island chapel, in its current form, is a large, permanent masonry structure built of buff Indiana limestone between 1905 and 1906.
It was a replacement for a deteriorating 1847 wooden chapel, representing a significant investment in a more durable and imposing building.
In stark contrast, the Chapel of the Centurion at Fort Monroe is a wood-frame Gothic Revival building, completed in 1858 and consecrated in 1858.

It was the original chapel from its inception and has remained in continuous use without replacement, making it a rare and invaluable artifact of 19th-century American ecclesiastical architecture on a military post.

The Governors Island chapel originated from the organized efforts of the Episcopal Church and Trinity Parish, with initial funding coming from donors and the personal contributions of chaplain John McVickar.
Its establishment was a response to the needs of a growing military population.
The Fort Monroe chapel has a more dramatic and personal origin story.

Its construction was directly funded by private subscription led by Lieutenant Julian McAllister, who survived a fatal laboratory explosion at the fort and attributed his safety to divine intervention.
His role as the principal contributor provides a compelling human element to the chapel's history, linking its foundation to a moment of profound personal faith and gratitude.
This narrative of a single officer's vow gives the chapel a unique and intimate backstory compared to the more institutionalized founding of its New York counterpart.

The Governors Island chapel, designed by Charles C. Haight, showcases a robust English Gothic style of the late 19th century, characterized by its massive limestone construction, a prominent three-story tower, and numerous stained glass windows.
Haight's design incorporated subtle military motifs, likely reflecting his own background and the chapel's setting on a former army base.
The Fort Monroe chapel, designed by the celebrated architect Richard Upjohn, embodies the refined elegance of the mid-19th-century Gothic Revival movement.
Its simpler wood-frame construction belies its artistic importance, particularly due to the presence of three stained-glass windows attributed to Louis Comfort Tiffany, a master of the medium.
The chapel on Governors Island has undergone a complete transformation from a military chapel to a public cultural venue.
After being inactive for worship since the Coast Guard's departure in 1996, it has been repurposed as a site for contemporary art installations, such as Jacob Hashimoto’s 'The Eclipse'.
This adaptive reuse aligns with the broader redevelopment of Governors Island into a public park and cultural destination, managed by the Governors Island Preservation and Education Corporation.
In contrast, the chapel at Fort Monroe continues its original function as an active place of worship.

As of September 2024, it remains in active use for civilian religious services, maintaining its role as a spiritual center for the community connected to the former military base, now a national monument.

Their paths of ownership also diverge; the Governors Island chapel was transferred to the city and then reclaimed by its original church owner, Trinity Church, which now manages it as a historic asset.

The Fort Monroe chapel, meanwhile, remains on government property, with its sacramental records handled by the Archdiocese for the Military Services, illustrating a different model of stewardship for a chapel on active-duty land.
The chapel on Governors Island in New York City has successfully navigated a transition from a functional place of worship to a preserved historic landmark and a dynamic public cultural venue.
Following the U.S. Coast Guard's departure from Governors Island in 1996, the chapel became inactive for regular religious services.
Its historical significance ensured its preservation.
As part of the Governors Island National Historic Landmark District and New York City Historic District, the chapel is protected and maintained as a key component of the island's heritage.
Ownership reverted to Trinity Church, which has since managed the property.
Recognizing the potential of the space, the chapel has been repurposed for contemporary use.
It is now publicly accessible and serves as a venue for art installations and cultural programming, a role that aligns with the island's transformation into a major public park and arts destination.
Notably, the chapel hosted Jacob Hashimoto’s 'The Eclipse', a suspended monochrome disk installation adapted from the 57th Venice Biennale, as part of the Governors Island Art Fair programming.
This adaptive reuse demonstrates a creative approach to preservation, ensuring the building remains a vibrant and relevant part of the community while honoring its past.

The chapel's architectural integrity has been assessed by professionals like the Architectural Preservation Studio, which conducted a comprehensive conditions evaluation, including laser-scanning documentation to create precise drawings for future conservation efforts.
This commitment to preservation ensures that the chapel will continue to stand as a significant example of 19th-century ecclesiastical architecture for future generations.
In contrast, the Chapel of the Centurion at Fort Monroe has maintained its core function as a place of active worship, adapting to the changing landscape of Fort Monroe itself.

Fort Monroe, once a sprawling U.S. Army base, was decommissioned and transformed into a combined National Monument and Presidential Site managed by the National Park Service and the Fort Monroe Authority.
Despite this significant change in administration and purpose for the surrounding area, the chapel has continued its uninterrupted service as a place of worship.
As of September 2024, it remains in active use for civilian religious services, fulfilling its original mission.
This continuity is remarkable, especially considering the chapel's age and its location within a complex undergoing major redevelopment.
The chapel's status is further secured by its unique administrative arrangement with the Archdiocese for the Military Services (AMS).

While the physical building is owned by the U.S. government, the AMS maintains canonical oversight and centralizes all sacramental records performed within it, ensuring that the chapel's religious functions are properly documented and sustained.
This partnership between a civilian governing body and a specialized ecclesiastical authority allows the chapel to operate effectively on military land.

The chapel's physical condition has been maintained through periodic restoration projects, including a major effort in 1968-1969 that cost $200,000 and was meticulously researched to preserve its historical authenticity.
This ongoing commitment to preservation and active use underscores the chapel's enduring importance to the community and its successful integration into the new civilian identity of Fort Monroe.

Inscription. ![Image 2](https://www.hmdb.org/SpeakIcon.png)    
During the first seven decades of American military use of Governors Island, there was no post chapel. In 1844, a Columbia College Episcopal Reverend, John M. McVickar, was commissioned post chaplain. His tireless efforts, combined with the sponsorship of his family and Trinity Church in Manhattan, led to the construction of a sizable wood frame chapel in 1847. This Episcopalian chapel was located just behind and to the right of where you are standing. By 1868, the Army elected to stop providing chaplains to the Island, leading Trinity Church to adopt the chapel into its Manhattan parish and provide its own chaplain.Reverend Edmund Banks Smith arrived in 1904 and energetically spearheaded the construction of a new masonry building to replace the original wood chapel, then in disrepair. The current English Gothic Style church was dedicated in 1906; and, like the original, was named after a soldier and early convert to Christianity, St. Cornelius the Centurion. Trinity Church retains ownership of the chapel to this day. Eventually, facilities for further religious services were made available to Island residents. The Our Lady of the

St. Cornelius the Centurion
===========================

February 5, 2014

News and Notes

_February 7 is the feast day of Cornelius the Centurion in the Episcopal calendar. In honor of his feast, here's a little background on the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion, one of the two remaining chapels of Trinity Parish._

![Image 12: Original St. Cornelius Chapel](https://trinitychurchnyc.org/sites/default/files/styles/content_width_100/public/2021-05/OriginalStCornelius.jpg?itok=4suZxlAc)

From the Archives of Trinity Church Wall Street

_The original Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion_

The Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion was built on Governors Island, a military outpost in New York Harbor, in 1846 through the efforts of the army chaplain, the Rev. John McVickar. Trinity Church provided McVickar and his successors with continuous support. By 1866, the War Department stopped providing chaplains to Governor’s Island. Trinity Church offered to maintain a chaplain at her own cost if the army would agree to place the chapel under the parish’s control. St. Cornelius became a part of Trinity Parish as a free chapel in 1868.

![Image 13: Consecration of the 2nd St. Cornelius Chapel](https://trinitychurchnyc.org/sites/default/files/styles/content_width_100/public/2021-05/ConsecrationStCornelius.jpg?itok=Z5u3lmDX)

From the Archives of Trinity Church Wall Street

_The consecration of the second Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion_

The Parish replaced the small wooden church with a new chapel designed by Charles C. Haight in 1906. In 1924, the agreement between the Army and Trinity was modified so that the Army paid the chaplain’s salary while Trinity maintained the building. St. Cornelius’ chaplains were honorary vicars and part of parish clergy. A 1954 agreement allowed chaplains from other Protestant denominations to use St. Cornelius to conduct services. This arrangement lasted until 1966, when the army turned over control of Governor’s Island to the U.S. Coast Guard. Under the Coast Guard, the Navy Chaplain Corps had the responsibility of assigning chaplains.

In the early 1970s, Trinity parish discontinued ordinary maintenance and janitorial services for St. Cornelius, but it continued to assist with major maintenance and provide insurance coverage

In 1980, the parish and St. Cornelius reached an agreement by which Trinity would lease the chapel to the U.S. Government for $1 per year. Then in 1986, Trinity donated the chapel to the U.S. Government, under the stipulation that it would revert to the parish if the government ceased to own the land underlying the chapel or to use the building as a military chapel. The Coast Guard vacated Governor’s Island in 1996, and Trinity regained ownership of the chapel, which is no longer in use.

![Image 14: Flags at St. Cornelius](https://trinitychurchnyc.org/sites/default/files/styles/content_width_100/public/2021-05/FlagsStCornelius.jpg?itok=6O3jvRkM)

From the Archives of Trinity Church Wall Street

_In the 1920s, flags displayed at St. Cornelius were restored. We loved this photo and are researching the flags and the restoration process. We'll report back soon!_

Saint of the Day – 20 October – Saint Cornelius the Centurion (1st Century)
===========================================================================

Posted on [October 20, 2021October 19, 2021](https://anastpaul.com/2021/10/20/saint-of-the-day-20-october-saint-cornelius-the-centurion-1st-century/) by [AnaStpaul](https://anastpaul.com/author/anastpaul/)

Saint of the Day – 20 October – Saint Cornelius the Centurion (1st Century) traditionally believed to have become the First Bishop of Caesarea,  
a Roman Centurion who is considered to be the one of first Gentile to convert to the Faith, (along with the conversion and Baptism of the Ethiopian eunuch – Acts 8). as related in Acts of the Apostles 10:1-49. The Baptism of Cornelius and his household, is an important event in the history of the early Church, for it points to the first century use of infant Baptism.

[![Image 2](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/st-cornelius-the-centurion-with-st-peter-baptism_of_cornelius-1.jpg?w=457)](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/st-cornelius-the-centurion-with-st-peter-baptism_of_cornelius-1.jpg)

St Peter Baptising Cornelius, the Centurion, by Francesco Trevisani, 1709

“Now in Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a Centurion of the Cohort called the Italica, devout and God-fearing along with his whole household, who used to give alms generously to the Jewish people and pray to God constantly. One afternoon about three o’clock, he saw plainly in a vision, an Angel of God come in to him and say to him, “_Cornelius._” He looked intently at him and, seized with fear, said, “_What is it, sir_?” He said to him, “_Your prayers and almsgiving have ascended as a memorial offering before God. Now send some men to Joppa and summon one Simon who is called Peter. He is staying with another Simon, a tanner, who has a house by the sea._” When the Angel who spoke to him had left, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from his staff, explained everything to them and sent them to Joppa.

[![Image 3](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/gerbrand_van_den_eeckhout_-_vision_of_cornelius_the_centurion_-_walters_372492-1.jpg?w=1018)](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/gerbrand_van_den_eeckhout_-_vision_of_cornelius_the_centurion_-_walters_372492-1.jpg)

St Cornelius’ dream

The next day, while they were on their way and nearing the city, Peter went up to the roof terrace to pray at about noontime. He was hungry and wished to eat and while they were making preparations, he fell into a trance. He saw heaven opened and something resembling a large sheet coming down, lowered to the ground by its four corners. In it were all the earth’s four-legged animals and reptiles and the birds of the sky. A voice said to him, “_Get up, Peter. Slaughter and eat._” But Peter said, “_Certainly not, sir. For never have I eaten anything profane and unclean._” The voice spoke to him again, a second time, “_What God has made clean, you are not to call profane._” This happened three times and then the object was taken up into the sky.

[![Image 4](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/594px-domenico_fetti_-_peters_vision_of_a_sheet_with_animals_-_kunsthistorisches_museum_wien.jpg?w=594)](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/594px-domenico_fetti_-_peters_vision_of_a_sheet_with_animals_-_kunsthistorisches_museum_wien.jpg)

Domenico Fetti – St Peter’s vision of a sheet with animals

While Peter was in doubt about the meaning of the vision he had seen, the men sent by Cornelius asked for Simon’s house and arrived at the entrance. They called out inquiring whether Simon, who is called Peter, was staying there. As Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said \[to him\] “_There are three men here looking for you. So get up, go downstairs and accompany them without hesitation because I have sent them._” Then Peter went down to the men and said, “_I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your being here?_” They answered, “_Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, respected by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to summon you to his house and to hear what you have to say._” So he invited them in and showed them hospitality. The next day he got up and went with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa went with him.

On the following day he entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and, falling at his feet, paid him homage. Peter, however, raised him up, saying, “_Get up. I myself am also a human being._” While he conversed with him, he went in and found many people gathered together and said to them, “_You know that it is unlawful for a Jewish man to associate with, or visit, a Gentile but God has shown me that I should not call any person profane or unclean. And that is why I came without objection when sent for. May I ask, then, why you summoned me?_” Cornelius replied, “_Four days ago at this hour, three o’clock in the afternoon, I was at prayer in my house when suddenly a man in dazzling robes stood before me and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your almsgiving remembered before God. Send therefore, to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter. He is a guest in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea._‘ So I sent for you immediately and you were kind enough to come. _Now, therefore, we are all here in the presence of God to listen to all that you have been commanded by the Lord.”_

[![Image 5](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/bernardo_cavallino_-_st_peter_and_cornelius_the_centurion_-_wga04598-1.jpg?w=997)](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/bernardo_cavallino_-_st_peter_and_cornelius_the_centurion_-_wga04598-1.jpg)

St Peter at St Cornelius’ house

Then Peter proceeded to speak and said, “_In truth, I see that God shows no partiality. Rather, in every nation whoever fears him and acts uprightly is acceptable to him. You know the word \[that\] he sent to the Israelites as he proclaimed peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all, what has happened all over Judea, beginning in Galilee after the baptism that John preached, how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the holy Spirit and power. He went about doing good and healing all those oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.m We are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and (in) Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree. This man God raised (on) the third day and granted that he be visible, not to all the people but to us, the witnesses chosen by God in advance, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. He commissioned us to preach to the people and testify, that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him will receive forgiveness of sins through his name_.”

[![Image 6](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/st-cornelius-the-centurion-glass-1.jpg?w=535)](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/st-cornelius-the-centurion-glass-1.jpg)

While Peter was still speaking these things, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who were listening to the word. The circumcised believers who had accompanied Peter were astounded that the gift of the Holy Spirit should have been poured out on the Gentiles also, for they could hear them speaking in tongues and glorifying God. Then Peter responded, “_Can anyone withhold the water for baptising these people, who have received the Holy Spirit even as we have?_” He ordered them to be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they invited him to stay for a few days. ” – **Acts 10:1-49**

[![Image 7](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/the_centurion_le_centurion_-_james_tissot-wikimedia-cc2-1-1.jpg?w=1000)](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/the_centurion_le_centurion_-_james_tissot-wikimedia-cc2-1-1.jpg)

A Centurion by James Tissot (not necesarily St Cornelius)

[![Image 8](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/please-assist-peter-and-paul-no-1-17.png?w=254)](https://anastpaul.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/please-assist-peter-and-paul-no-1-17.png)

              Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion
			  (Episcopal)

			  Governors Island
			  New York Harbor
			  New York, N.Y. 10004

                    Organ Specifications:
					Present Chapel (since 1905)
					• Rodgers Instruments electronic (1990s)
					► II/6 M.P. Möller, Inc., Op. 8673 (1954)
					• II/18 Hook & Hastings, Op. 2115 (1906)
					Original Chapel (1847-1905)
					• unknown, if any

Governors Island is located in the New York Harbor, approximately one-half mile from Battery Park in Lower Manhattan and one-quarter mile from Brooklyn. Its waterfront offers some of the most dramatic and impressive vistas of the New York skyline and New York Harbor, including the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island. Physically, the Island changed greatly during the early twentieth century. Using rocks and dirt from the excavations for the Lexington Avenue Subway, the Army Corps of Engineers supervised the deposit of 4,787,000 cubic yards of fill on the south side of Governors Island, adding 103 acres of flat, treeless land by 1912, and bringing the total acreage of the Island to 172. The island has nearly 225 buildings, considerable open space, and recreational amenities. The northern half of the Island, consisting of approximately 92 acres, has been designated as both a National Historic Landmark District and a New York City Historic District, and features late 18th and early 19th century fortifications, pre-Civil War arsenal buildings, Victorian and Romanesque Revival housing, as well as early 20th century neo-classical architecture. Five buildings within the Historic District, including Fort Jay and Castle Williams, are individually listed in the National Register of Historic Places.
The Native Americans of the Manhattan region referred to the island as Pagganck (“Nut Island”) after the Island’s plentiful hickory, oak and chestnut trees. In June of 1637, Wouter Van Twiller, representative of Holland, purchased the island from the Native Americans of Manahatas for two ax heads, a string of beads, and a handful of nails. The Island, thereafter known as Noten Eylant or Nutten Island, was confiscated by the Dutch Government a year later. In 1664 the English captured New Amsterdam, renaming it New York, and took Nutten Island, which had been left unfortified by the Dutch. The island, however, switched hands between the British and the Dutch over the next 10 years until the British regained exclusive control of the island for the “benefit and accommodation of His Majesty's Governors.” Although it was not officially named until 1784, it thus came to be called Governors Island.

The island’s strategic location resulted in its use as a military facility by British and American forces for over 200 years. In 1794, with the country in need of a system of coastal defenses, construction began on Fort Jay, on high ground in the center of the Island. In 1800, New York transferred the Island to the United States government for military purposes. During the American Civil War, it was used for recruitment and as a prison for captured Confederate soldiers. Throughout World Wars I and II, the Island served as an important supply base for Army ground and air forces.

With the consolidation of U.S. Military forces in 1966, the island was transferred to the Coast Guard, making it  their largest installation. Governors Island served as a self-contained residential community, with an on-island population of approximately 3,500, and as a base of operations for the Atlantic Area Command and Maintenance and Logistics Command as well as the Captain of the Port of New York. In 1995, the Coast Guard closed its facilities on Governors Island and all residential personnel were relocated. President Clinton designated 22 acres of the island, including the two great forts, as the Governors Island National Monument in January 2001, and on April 1, 2002, it was announced that the United States of America would sell Governors Island to the people of New York for a nominal cost. On January 31, 2003, the island was transferred to the people of New York through the Governors Island Preservation and Education Corporation.

            Original chapel

The original chapel on Governors Island dates back to 1846 when the Rev. John McVickar, D.D., was appointed chaplain for the Army servicemen and their families on the island. Services were held under the trees in fair weather, and in the post headquarters at other times. Dr. McVickar soon campaigned for an adequate post chapel, but the Government was not accustomed to building chapels, nor was it willing to make an appropriation for the purpose. Dr. McVickar counted among his friends the Commander-in-Chief of the Army, General Scott, and shortly the  Government agreed to lease about 150 feet square on the south side of the island as a site for a chapel, subject to the exigencies of war. The chaplain set about raising private subscriptions for a chapel, and received a generous contribution from the corporation of Trinity Church, New York. In 1847, "a neat and tasteful church-like building of wood" was constructed after the chaplain's own plans from funds collected by himself. Thereafter, from 1846 to 1855, Trinity Church made an annual appropriation for its support, and in 1868, the chapel became part of Trinity Parish.

        Original chapel with new chapel at rear

By the beginning of the 20th century, the 1847 chapel was in such disrepair that Trinity deemed it unsalvageable. In 1905, the Army accepted Trinity's offer to build a new chapel, and in October, 1905, the cornerstone was laid for the present building. Just a year later, on October 19, 1906, the new chapel with the old name, the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion, was dedicated by Bishop David Greer, assisted by the clergy of Trinity Parish, New York. The music for the occasion was furnished by the choir of Trinity Church, under the direction of Mr. Victor Baier, and by the choir of the post chapel, under the direction of Lt. A. F. Halpin (retired), the post organist.

The new chapel was designed by Charles C. Haight in the English Gothic style of the 14th century. It is a cruciform structure of buff Indiana  limestone with a massive tower, nave, transepts, chancel, and side chapel. The total length is 106 feet and the greatest width 70 feet. Carved oak clergy and choir seats are provided, while the nave and St. Albans Chapel have chairs. The clergy and choir sacristies and the organ are on the south side of the chancel. Under the chancel is a mortuary chapel, and the roof of this and the entire crypt is vaulted with flat Italian tile. Until recently the chapel housed historically significant battle flags and other symbolic relics.

Governors Island has two other chapels: Our Lady, Star of the Sea (Roman Catholic, built in 1942) and a Jewish Chapel.

Cornelius
=========

Centurion of the Italic cohort, whose conversion at Caesarea with his household is related in Acts, x
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

2021-09-28T09:17:35

Share

🖨️🔗

![Image 8](https://cdn.catholic.com/wp-content/uploads/oce-scans/thumbs/0400425.jpg)

Click to enlarge

_Cornelius (Kornelios_), a centurion of the Italic cohort, whose conversion at [Caesarea](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/caesarea) with his house-hold is related in Acts, x. The Roman name Cornelius would indicate that he was either a member of the distinguished _gens Cornelia_, or a descendant of one of its freedmen—most likely the latter. The cohort in which he was centurion was probably the _Cohors II Italica civi um, Romanorum_, which a recently discovered inscription proves to have been stationed in [Syria](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/syria) before A.D. 69. The description of Cornelius as “a religious man, and fearing [God](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/god) giving much alms to the people” \[i.e. the Jews (cf. x, 22)\], shows that he was one of those gentiles commonly, though incorrectly, called proselytes of the gate, who worshipped the one true [God](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/god) and observed some of the prescriptions of the Mosaic [Law](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/law), but who were not affiliated to the Jewish community by circumcision. He was certainly not a full proselyte (Acts, x, 28, 34 sq., 45; xi, 3). The baptism of Cornelius is an important event in the history of the Early [Church](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/church-the). The gates of the [Church](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/church-the), within which thus far only those who were circumcised and observed the [Law](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/law) of [Moses](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/moses) had been admitted, were now thrown open to the uncircumcised [Gentiles](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/gentiles) without the obligation of submitting to the Jewish ceremonial laws. The innovation was disapproved by the Jewish Christians at [Jerusalem](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/jerusalem) (Acts, xi, 2, 3); but when Peter had related his own and Cornelius’s vision and how the [Holy Ghost](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/holy-ghost) had come down upon the new converts, opposition ceased (Acts, xi, 4-18) except on the part of a few extremists. The matter was finally settled at the Council of [Jerusalem](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/jerusalem) (Acts, xv). According to one tradition Cornelius became [Bishop](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/bishop) of [Caesarea](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/caesarea); according to another, [Bishop](https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/bishop) of Scepsis in Mysia.

F. BECHTEL

**Cornelius** ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Κορνήλιος, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Greek "Romanization of Greek"): _Kornḗlios_; [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _Cornēlius_ [\[kɔrˈneː.li.ʊs\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Latin "Help:IPA/Latin"); fl. 1st century AD) was a [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") [centurion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centurion "Centurion") who is considered by some [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") to be the first [Gentile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentile "Gentile") to [convert to the faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_to_Christianity "Conversion to Christianity"), as related in [Acts of the Apostles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_the_Apostles "Acts of the Apostles") (see [Ethiopian eunuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_eunuch "Ethiopian eunuch") for the competing tradition). The baptism of Cornelius is an important event in the history of the early Christian church. He may have belonged to the [gens Cornelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gens_Cornelia "Gens Cornelia"), a prominent Roman family.

Cornelius was a centurion in the [Cohors II Italica Civium Romanorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohors_II_Italica_Civium_Romanorum "Cohors II Italica Civium Romanorum"), mentioned as _Cohors Italica_ in the [Vulgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate "Vulgate").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-4) He was stationed in [Caesarea Maritima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesarea_Maritima "Caesarea Maritima"), the capital of Roman [Iudaea province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaea_/(Roman_province/) "Judaea (Roman province)").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-cathen-5) He is depicted in the [New Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Testament "New Testament") as a [God-fearing man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God-fearer "God-fearer")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-6) who always prayed and was full of good works and deeds of [alms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alms "Alms"). Cornelius receives a vision in which an [angel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel "Angel") of God tells him that his prayers have been heard; he understands that he has been chosen for a higher alternative. The angel then instructs Cornelius to send the men of his household to [Joppa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaffa "Jaffa"), where they will find [Simon Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Peter "Saint Peter"), who is residing with a [tanner by the name of Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_the_Tanner_/(New_Testament/) "Simon the Tanner (New Testament)") ([Acts 10:5ff](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible_/(King_James/)/Acts#10:5 "s:Bible (King James)/Acts")).

The [conversion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_to_Christianity "Conversion to Christianity") of Cornelius comes after [a separate vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%27s_vision_of_a_sheet_with_animals "Peter's vision of a sheet with animals") given to Simon Peter ([Acts 10:10–16](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible_/(King_James/)/Acts#10:10 "s:Bible (King James)/Acts")). In the vision, Simon Peter sees all manner of beasts and fowl being lowered from [Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaven "Heaven") in a sheet. A voice commands Simon Peter to eat. When he objects to eating those animals that are [unclean according to Mosaic Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashrut "Kashrut"), the voice tells him not to call unclean that which God has cleansed.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-oca-7)

When Cornelius' men arrive, Simon Peter understands that through this vision the Lord had commanded him to preach the Word of God to the Gentiles. Peter accompanies Cornelius' men back to Caesarea.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-oca-7) When Cornelius meets Simon Peter, he falls at Peter's feet. Simon Peter raises the centurion, and the two men share their visions. Simon Peter tells of [Jesus' ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Jesus "Ministry of Jesus") and the [Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection_of_Jesus "Resurrection of Jesus"); the [Holy Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Spirit "Holy Spirit") descends on everyone at the gathering. The [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jew "Jew") among the group are amazed that Cornelius and other [uncircumcised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumcision_controversy_in_early_Christianity "Circumcision controversy in early Christianity") should begin [speaking in tongues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaking_in_tongues "Speaking in tongues"), praising God. Thereupon Simon Peter commands that Cornelius and his followers, "kinsmen and near friends", be [baptized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism "Baptism").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-cocn-8) The controversial aspect of Gentile conversion is taken up later at the [Council of Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Jerusalem "Council of Jerusalem") ([Acts 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_15 "Acts 15")).

### Religious situation of Judea

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cornelius_the_Centurion&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Religious situation of Judea")\]

Taking into account that Judea had been within the Hellenic orbit since the conquest of [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great"), there was time for wise men and philosophers, both Greek and Jewish, to exchange knowledge, thus beginning the syncretism between [Hellenism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_religion "Hellenistic religion") and [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism "Judaism"), a phenomenon that occurred in the rest of his empire. Later with the arrival of the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") (already Hellenized), there were no problems of [religious tolerance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_tolerance "Religious tolerance") (except in the case of the [Zealots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealots "Zealots")), since thanks to the _[interpretatio graeca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpretatio_graeca "Interpretatio graeca")_ exported by the [Macedonians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_/(ancient_kingdom/) "Macedonia (ancient kingdom)"), it was possible to identify [Caelus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caelus "Caelus") (Roman god) or [Uranus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus_/(mythology/) "Uranus (mythology)") (his Greek equivalent) and [Yahweh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahweh "Yahweh") as the Supreme [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God "God"), allowing conversion cases like Cornelius.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-11)

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Gerbrand_van_den_Eeckhout_-_Vision_of_Cornelius_the_Centurion_-_Walters_372492.jpg/250px-Gerbrand_van_den_Eeckhout_-_Vision_of_Cornelius_the_Centurion_-_Walters_372492.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gerbrand_van_den_Eeckhout_-_Vision_of_Cornelius_the_Centurion_-_Walters_372492.jpg)

In this painting by [Gerbrand van den Eeckhout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerbrand_van_den_Eeckhout "Gerbrand van den Eeckhout") an angel appears to the Roman centurion Cornelius. The angel tells him to seek out St. Peter.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-12) The Walters Art Museum.

> Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we?

— Acts 10:47

Cornelius is considered to be one of the first gentile converts to Christianity.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-13) The baptism of Cornelius is an important event in the history of the early Christian church, along with the conversion and baptism of the [Ethiopian eunuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_eunuch "Ethiopian eunuch"). The Christian church was first formed around the original disciples and followers of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus"), all of whom—including Jesus—were [Galilean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean "Galilean"), except for [Judas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judas_Iscariot "Judas Iscariot") who was Judean. Males in the Judean community were Jews: they were circumcised and observed the [Law of Moses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/613_commandments "613 commandments"). The reception of Cornelius sparked a debate among the leaders of the new community of followers of Jesus, culminating in the decision to allow Gentiles to become Christians without conforming to Jewish requirements for circumcision, as recounted in [Acts 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_15 "Acts 15").

His feast day on the new [Martyrologium Romanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martyrologium_Romanum "Martyrologium Romanum") is 20 October. He is commemorated in the Orthodox tradition on 13 September.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-oca-7) Cornelius is honored on the [liturgical calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendar_of_saints_/(Episcopal_Church/) "Calendar of saints (Episcopal Church)") of the [Episcopal Church in the United States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_/(United_States/) "Episcopal Church (United States)") on [February 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_4 "February 4").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-teccalendar-2) The [Armenian Apostolic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Apostolic_Church "Armenian Apostolic Church") commemorates Cornelius on the Tuesday after the third Sunday of [Advent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advent "Advent").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-14)

Certain traditions hold Cornelius as becoming either the first [bishop of Caesarea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Caesarea "Bishop of Caesarea"), or the bishop of [Scepsis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scepsis "Scepsis") in [Mysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysia "Mysia").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-cathen-5)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-cocn-8) The Greek-French philosopher [Cornelius Castoriadis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_Castoriadis "Cornelius Castoriadis") was named after him.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-15) When [Governors Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governors_Island "Governors Island") in New York City was a military installation, the Episcopal Church maintained a [stone chapel there dedicated to him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion "Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-16)
